rows.en: Also in the other prophetic books from the time of the exile precious traces are found that point to various traditions which lived among the people from ancient times, and through which the statute of the Torah is broadened (Isaiah 58:13, and see above, ch. 5). For our purpose there is no need to bring all the details; but it is fitting to remark on one more matter, for two reasons. The first: because it interprets a statute in the Torah, and that interpretation was upheld and accepted by all the prophets down to the end of the days of the exile. The second reason is that it is one of the interpretations that in the course of time was abolished entirely. As regards the standing of the day of the new moon, or Rosh Ḥodesh, nothing clear is found in the Torah, and we do not know whether it has holiness like the other festivals of the year or not. It is only said that on the new moons special sacrifices are offered, as on the Sabbath and on the festivals (Numbers 28:11), and likewise that the trumpets are blown over the sacrifices as on a festival (ibid. 10:10). But from the words of the prophets we learn that they used to celebrate the day of the new moon. Already in the days of the prophet Elisha the good among the people used to go to the prophet to inquire of the Lord on the day of the new moon as on the Sabbath day (2 Kings 5:23)⚠1, and this is a sign that it was a day of rest. Likewise Isaiah calls it a holy convocation, like the Sabbath day (Isaiah 1:13), and Ezekiel too makes it a holy convocation on which all the people of the land shall come to bow down before the Lord (Ezekiel 46:1). And not only was the day of the new moon a festival with a special divine service on it, but they also refrained from work on it. For they called the day before the new moon "the working day" in contrast to the day of the new moon, which is the day of rest (1 Samuel 20:19, and see Targum Jonathan and the Septuagint, and the Babylonian Talmud Megillah 22b with Rashi's commentary), and on it they refrained from buying and selling (Amos 8:5). From all this it is clearly seen that they rested on Rosh Ḥodesh as on a festival. Without doubt they interpreted the statute in the Torah in this way: since the day is distinguished by special sacrifices, it therefore has the holiness of a festival. But this interpretation did not endure in the course of time; perhaps already after they returned from the exile they no longer kept it, but made the day of the new moon like the intermediate days of a festival, and refrained from doing work on it only when the work was not urgent (see Megillah, ibid.); and in the course of time the strap was loosened altogether, and the custom remained only among the women (Ḥagigah 18a and the Tosafot there, and Yerushalmi Ta'anit ch. 1). Now if we cast our eye over all the traces of the Torah that we have mentioned so far, we find that it is no empty thing that our ancestors handed down to us: that besides the statutes and ordinances written in the book of the Torah there were still among the people ancient traditions, statutes and customs that were not written in the book. On such traditions several of the written statutes were founded. It is likewise true and established that the teachings and statutes that have reached us in writing were interpreted in all ages, from the days of old, wherever they needed interpretation. We have also seen that several interpretations changed in the course of the times and the generations. It is likewise clear that many times there is a contradiction between the sense of the statutes in an early time and their sense among the later generations; but sometimes agreement between them is also found. On this basis we can determine with clarity that many of the ancient interpretations endured and have reached us, and that they agree with several interpretations that we have today. And indeed it has also become known to us that the study of the Torah went step by step. Among the prophets of the first generations, until the end of the days of the Temple, it had a different character from what it had from then on. In the days of the exile they began to be more exact in the practice of the statutes and in their examination, and this was the time of transition. From the beginning of the time that came after it, the study of the Torah reached a new stage: exactness and examination grew from day to day and in each and every generation. And this new stage began from the time of their return from the exile to the rest and to the inheritance [Deuteronomy 12:9].

1.note: The verse about going to the prophet on the new moon and Sabbath is 2 Kings 4:23, not 5:23.

rows.en: The state of Torah study at the beginning of their return from the exile; the work of the Scribes in regard to the Hebrew language;
the sayings of the Scribes and their ordinances; the antiquity of the halakhah and its expansion; Simeon the Just, of the remnant of the Men of the Great Assembly.
The state of Torah study at the beginning of their return from the exile.

About fifty years had passed since the day of the exile from the land (A.M. 3402)⚠1, and the signs that the prophets had foretold long before [Isaiah 41:23] about Babylon and its kingdom had come; not one of them had failed. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms [Isaiah 13:19], fell at the feet of the Persian conqueror; her pride was brought down to Sheol [Isaiah 14:11], and her king was slain among the slain. In this downfall Israel saw the end of its exile and hope for its redemption. Seeing that the Lord had fulfilled the word of His servants the prophets concerning Babylon and its kingdom, the hope grew strong in them that the vision which the prophets had seen for good concerning Judah and Jerusalem would also be fulfilled, and that the time of their deliverance was near. Indeed, the days did not grow long before Darius the Mede, under whose reign Babylon had been conquered, died, and Cyrus, who had conquered it, rose to the kingship in his place, and the kingdom of Babylon came under his sceptre. He was a kindly king to Israel. In the first year of his reign he gave them permission to go up to the land of their birth and to build a house to the Lord in Jerusalem. Then many of Israel made the effort to go up, and they went up. This ascent was the first step that "these, the people of the Lord" [Ezekiel 36:20] took to fulfil the great and holy destiny for which this people had been designated from of old: to be a banner to many nations. Deep, deep within them was sunk the memory of the hardships and sorrows that had passed over them for a long time for their walking in the abominable statutes of the nations and in ordinances by which one does not live [Ezekiel 20:25]. The memory of all this was a lesson to them, to make their latter end good. The idea of their mission filled the heart of the best of the nation, and it is engraved with an iron pen [Job 19:24] in all the holy words that remain to us as a blessing from the men of wonder who lived and worked in the exile. All the prophecies and words of comfort from that time depict this idea in the robes of sublime eloquence. Their desire and aim was not to establish a kingdom like the kingdoms of the earth, but to establish their holy religion and to give it standing and survival until the end of days. At the head of the first who went up stood Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, of the seed of the house of David, and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. With them went up forty-two thousand three hundred and sixty men, besides the women and the children, and besides their menservants and maidservants (A.M. 3452). When they reached their land, all the people gathered to Jerusalem, and the heads rose up and built an altar to offer burnt offerings on it; but the house was not yet founded until the second year of their going up. Then days and years passed and they could not complete the building, for they had many adversaries among the people of the land, who brought an evil report of them to the kings of Persia. Above all the Kutim [Samaritans], whom the king of Assyria had settled in the cities of Samaria, harassed and denounced them. Therefore the building was held back until the second year of Darius the Persian (A.M. 3467). Then the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo stirred their hearts to found the house anew. It seems that in the days of Darius their adversaries were not hostile to them, or achieved nothing with Darius, for he was a kindly king. Yet the prophets kept silent in the first year of his reign, because, as it appears, that year was a year of drought, and therefore it was not the right time for building the house (Haggai 1:6; 2:17). From the government too they obtained permission to complete the building, and with doubled strength they now worked at the holy work, and in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the building was completed. The completion was on the third of the month of Adar, and they at once made the dedication of the house with joy; without doubt they made it at the beginning of the month of Nisan, like the dedication of the altar in the Tabernacle. But in the sacrifices that they offered for the dedication of the house they did not do as is written, and they departed from Scripture both in the kinds of the sacrifices and in their number (Ezra 6:17). And indeed, even though the service returned to Zion and the sanctuary rose from the heaps of dust, the religious spirit that the prophets had sought had not yet returned, and many days still passed for Israel without Torah [2 Chronicles 15:3]; and no traces of Torah study at all are found in all the first days and years, from the day they went up in the first ascent led by Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, until the days of the reign of King Artaxerxes (A.M. 3523)⚠2, under whose reign the second ascent took place.

1.note: Read as a year from Creation (3,000 + 402); likewise ג"א תנ"ב, תס"ז, תקמ"א below.

2.note: Printed תקב"ג, which is not a regular numeral (image checked); probably תקכ"ג = 3523.

rows.en: This work of reviving the spirit of religion among his people was reserved for one of the men of wonder, who was called to plant the plantings of the Torah in the vineyard of the Lord of hosts [Isaiah 5:7]. This exalted man was Ezra son of Seraiah, of the family of the priests, the fourteenth generation from Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron the priest (Ezra 7:1–4). A multitude of honorable virtues were a crown of glory on his head; but one virtue surpassed them all [Proverbs 31:29]: his strength and power in the Torah of Moses, to teach the people statute and ordinance (ibid. 7:10). In the seventh year of the reign of Artaxerxes, Ezra obtained permission from the king to go up with a large number of his people to the land of Judah, to the inheritance of their fathers. When he spoke before the king to ask of him permission for his people to return to their land, he based his request only on the cornerstone of religion; his whole desire was only to bring his people back to the religion of their fathers and to the Torah. In the copy of the letter that the king gave into Ezra's hand, the purpose of the ascent is also set out: to appoint judges and officers who would judge between case and case in Jerusalem, for all who know the law of God, and to teach whoever does not know it (ibid. 7:25). For this reason too the later sages compared Ezra's ascent to Moses' ascent of Mount Sinai, for the purpose of both was to teach the people Torah (Sanhedrin 21b; Tosefta ibid., ch. 4). And they said of him that he founded the Torah a second time after it had been forgotten in his days (Sifre Ekev, piska 48; Sukkah 20a), and they raised his rank above that of Aaron the priest, until they said of him: had Aaron been alive, Ezra would have been greater than he in his time (Midrash Kohelet). Yet although Ezra was of the family of Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron the priest, and a shoot from the stock of Zadok, of whose family none went astray when Israel went astray [Ezekiel 48:11], and he stood at the head of those who went up, with all the best of the house of Israel in his hand, nevertheless we do not find that the desire seized him to take for himself the high priesthood, which he could easily have filled, since every man of Israel followed him (see Song of Songs Rabbah on the verse "I arose"). But Ezra did a great thing in refraining from serving in the high priesthood. This is in keeping with what we have seen: that in all the generations the forgetting of the Torah came mostly through the fault of the priests. Therefore it was necessary to remove the chief causes that brought harm to the Torah and its study, and this could be achieved by working for its spread and for its study. And this effort could be strengthened only if the custody of the Torah were not reserved to the priests, as it had been in former days. The attainment of the aim of raising the horn of the Torah and strengthening religion was the goal of Ezra's life. In the keeping of the statutes of the Torah he saw the foundation for the survival of the nation, and therefore Ezra did not wish to reach his goal by virtue of being a priest, but by virtue of being a sage who had set his heart to seek the Torah of the Lord [Ezra 7:10]. Ezra the priest was called a scribe (sofer) because of his skill in the art of writing, and he used to write Torah scrolls to distribute them in Jacob [Genesis 49:7]. This virtue, of being a master of the art of writing, is a small thing in our eyes today, but in those days it was precious. There is no hint that before that time there were copies of the book of the Torah of Moses in the hands of the people. King Jehoshaphat sent men through the cities of Judah to teach the people Torah, and the envoys, the teachers, took with them the book of the Torah of the Lord (2 Chronicles 17:7–9). From this we can judge that no book was found in the hands of the people, for otherwise they would not have needed to carry a Torah scroll in their bosom from city to city in all the cities of Israel. And after this, in the days of King Josiah son of Amon, there was no copy even in the king's hand (2 Kings 22). But Ezra was a wonderful master of the art of writing and a ready scribe in the Torah [Ezra 7:6], and he did his work with speed and wonderful skill. And since this skill was found only among the sages, the sages too were therefore called by the name Scribes (Soferim), until the name ḥakham ("sage") and the name sofer ("scribe") were equal in their meaning. This name suits the teachers in another respect too: that they taught from the book.{v1_04_02:1} The masters of the Talmud gave the name Soferim yet another sense, and say that the sages of that generation were called Soferim because they counted (sofrim) the letters of the Torah, or because the Soferim made the Torah into counted sections (sefurot sefurot).{v1_04_03:1} But whether the Scribes of this time, with Ezra at their head, were the authors of such works still needs proof. It seems more likely that such explanations have only the value of aggadah, and that in this too they went their usual way of explaining matters or names according to their need on the basis of new concepts. In truth the name sofer means only one who writes or copies books, or one who learns from the book. The name sofer is a synonym of mevin ("one who understands") (1 Chronicles 26:32)⚠1; and mevin is a common epithet describing the teacher, and it is mentioned in contrast to talmid ("pupil") (ibid. 25:8). From this name we recognize the character of their teaching: that they taught with reflection, adding to the words of the book an explanation to make its matter understood. But when Ezra came to Jerusalem at the head of the second group that went up, the time was not yet fit to make the spread of Torah study the chief of his work, for the religious state that he found in the land of Judah was still bad; and the beginning of his work was to separate the people from the mixture with the peoples of the land, for many of Israel, even of the priests and the Levites, had mingled with them (Ezra 9). But many days still passed, and his desire did not prosper in his hand as he had hoped, until in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes great help reached him. Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, who was cupbearer to the king, obtained permission to build the walls of Jerusalem and the ruined city. The king commanded him to be governor in the land of Judah. This man, who loved his people and feared God, stood at Ezra's right hand to support him in his holy desire. At that time (A.M. 3541), on the first of the seventh month, which is the Day of Remembrance, all the people assembled, and Ezra read before them in the book of the Torah of the Lord; and on the second day too the heads of the fathers' houses of all the people, the priests and the Levites, gathered to Ezra, and he instructed them in the words of the Torah (Nehemiah 8). The manner and way of their teaching was this: they read in the book of the Torah of God distinctly, as it is written and in its own language, and gave the sense with understanding and with fitting reflection, to explain it to the hearers, and caused them to understand the reading (ibid. 8:8). And indeed, included in the explanation and the understanding was also a translation of the book into the language to which part of the people was accustomed (Megillah 3a; Nedarim 37a). For many of the Jews who had grown up in Babylonia, and also the Jews who lived in the land of Judah, were accustomed to speak in the language of the peoples among whom they lived (ibid. 13:24). Already from ancient times it was the custom to read in public words of moral instruction and reproof from the prophets, and the reading of portions from the books of the prophets, which we call the haftarah, is very ancient.{v1_04_03:2} It is possible that at that time they began to read in the Torah on the days of assembly, on the Sabbaths and on the festivals of the year, and one would stand and translate. In any case it is clear that the great aim on which Ezra set his eye was to teach the people knowledge of the statutes of the Torah, so that they would know with right understanding the way in which they should walk. The way that Ezra and the Mevinim chose for themselves when they wished to interpret the books of the ancients we can recognize if we pay attention to some of our holy writings that were composed on the basis of written sources by authors who preceded them. For there are writings among the Holy Scriptures whose authors drew from old books, and they did not use these sources as written and in their own words, in the way of copyists, without investigation and criticism; rather, they reflected on the sources before them and expounded them according to their own opinions and according to the concepts of their time, or also according to the received meaning. A faithful witness to this will be the book of Chronicles that we have. The author of this book himself testifies in scattered places that he drew his narratives from old sources.{v1_04_04:1} These sources were written. Many were lost, and we do not know what became of them. Most of the Holy Scriptures that we have today were also among his sources, and in all the places where his sources are open before us as they were before him, we see that he departed from them in various ways and chose a way of his own in the sense of the deeds and events. Even where the Torah was the source of his narratives, he appears as one who interprets the words of the Torah. In several places he adds words to the words of the source, sometimes changes the wording, and expands the phrases, so that it appears that his intention is to interpret the sources from which he drew his words. And if we pay attention to the character of his additions, expansions and changes, by which he wished to give added explanation to the original source that lay before him, we easily find that he turned his attention to three kinds of interpretation. The first: the effort to reconcile apparent contradictions and to shed light on obscure passages.{v1_04_04:2} The second: that he describes the words of the ancient book according to his own opinion and understanding and according to the concepts of his time.{v1_04_04:3} The third: that he tries to explain the words of the ancient book by seeking out their reason and their cause.{v1_04_04:4} From this we can come to know the way in which they went at that time in their interpretations, and in what manner they used ancient books. For the author of the book of Chronicles lived and wrote his book in the third generation after Ezra.{v1_04_04:5} Therefore, when we see that this author was accustomed to go deep and reflect on the sources that lay before him, tried to reconcile the obscurities and the contradictions, expounded them according to his opinions and the concepts of his time, and gave a reason and a cause for a matter that the ancient source reported plainly and without a reason, so too we may judge rightly that the way of the sages of the first generations, who are the generations of the Mevinim and the Scribes, was of this kind: when they gave understanding of Scripture, their understanding of it was not only the explanation of the words, or a translation according to the plain sense of the words as written, in the way of the masters of Scripture; rather, they went deep into it, straightened and reconciled what was obscure and difficult, interpreted according to their own opinion and according to the concepts of their time wherever they had no received interpretation or where it did not suffice for their need, and tried to teach their hearers, and make them understand, the reason of the matters and their grounds.

1.note: The verse with מבין וסופר (David's uncle Jonathan) is 1 Chronicles 27:32.

footnotes.en: These are the words of the verse there: "Sigh in silence, make no mourning for the dead; bind your headdress upon you, and put your shoes on your feet, and do not cover your upper lip, and do not eat the bread of men" [Ezekiel 24:17]. From this it appears that he distinguished between the inner mourning, which is in the heart, and the outward signs of mourning. He was commanded not to perform the outward signs, but he may grieve for his wife in his heart. Perhaps these words of the prophet are the source of what is said in the Mishnah, that even where one is not permitted to mourn, he grieves, for grief (aninut) is only in the heart (Sanhedrin 46b); and see what I wrote in my book *Mishpat Leshon ha-Mishnah*, p. 48. As for the outward signs of mourning, the Torah has the uncovering of the head and the rending of the garments (Leviticus 21:10). In the opinion of some, the uncovering of the head is the same as the removal of the headdress [pe'er], and the matter of both is the removal of the turban (see the Septuagint translation; so too Rosenmüller and Michaelis understood it).

I will remark here on the statute of the impurity of priests: "And they shall come at no dead person to defile themselves, except for father and for mother, etc." [Ezekiel 44:25]; and in the Torah a phrase is added: "except for his kin, that is near to him" [Leviticus 21:2]. From the fact that he left out this phrase it appears that he did not think that it points to a particular relative, but that it is only a general term followed by a specification, where the specification explains the general term; and the prophet left out the general term because it suffices to list the particulars. But in the Talmud "his kin" (she'ero) is expounded: this is his wife (Yevamot 22b, 90b; Sifra Emor ch. 1). This midrash is necessarily late, and it seems that it is an offshoot of their midrash on inheritances, where they expounded she'ero as referring to the wife (Bava Batra 111b). Perhaps the Sadducees disputed this halakhah, that the husband inherits his wife, as they disputed other halakhot in the laws of inheritance (ibid. 116b), because they did not find the matters stated explicitly in the Torah; and the Pharisees wished to give it a hint from the Torah and found it in the word she'ero. Once she'ero had been explained as referring to the wife in one place, they necessarily had to expound the "she'ero" written in the law of the impurity of priests in this sense too. Therefore it seems that the halakhah that a priest defiles himself for his wife is late. It further seems that this halakhah was still weak in their hands even at a late time, as we see in the story of Joseph the priest, who did not want to defile himself for his wife, and his brothers the priests pushed him and defiled him against his will (Sifra Emor ch. 1; Zevaḥim 100a). And Josephus, *Antiquities*, part 1, book 3, ch. 12, likewise does not mention this.

See *Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11. In the Gemara it appears that sofer denotes one who teaches from the book, as in "the wage of a scribe and of a Mishnah teacher" (Yerushalmi Ḥagigah ch. 1). In the book *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 3, it is written that he was called "a ready scribe" because he occupied himself with the book of the Torah to interpret it; but this is not so: rather, he was called "a ready scribe" because of his speed in the art of writing, as in "my tongue is the pen of a ready scribe" (Psalms 45:2).

See Kiddushin 30a and Yerushalmi Shekalim ch. 5. They said of Ezra: just as he was a sofer in the words of the Torah (meaning, counting the letters), so he was a sofer in the words of the sages (meaning, [arranging them in] counted sections); and see Ḥagigah 15b and Sanhedrin 106b, which derive these two senses from the verse "Where is he that counted, where is he that weighed, where is he that counted the towers?" [Isaiah 33:18].

These are the words of the scholar Herzfeld (*Geschichte*, vol. 1, p. 132): "There is no doubt that in the exile set discourses were read before them on the days of holy convocation, from the earlier holy writings and also from those written in the exile; and it seems that most of the portions in the second part of Isaiah, etc., were written and kept for this purpose. And in the Epistle of Baruch 1:14 it says explicitly that the book which he sent to the exiles was so that they would read it, and for this reason he sent it to them, that they should read it on the Sabbaths and festivals." But from the Epistle of Baruch there is no proof, for it was written at a late time, as will be made clear further below, ch. 22.
